title: Global Justice and Cosmopolitanism
subtitle: Does justice stop at the border?
objectives: By the end you will be able to contrast cosmopolitan and statist views about the scope of justice
By the end you will be able to explain Pogge's argument that global poverty is a harm imposed through institutions, including the resource and borrowing privileges
By the end you will be able to reconstruct the main arguments for open borders and for the right to exclude
By the end you will be able to describe Nussbaum's capabilities approach and how it measures what people are able to do and be
hook:
Two babies are born on the same day. One arrives in Oslo, the other in a village in South Sudan. Neither has done anything to deserve anything. Yet the first can expect to live into her eighties, attend university and earn many times what the second will earn; the second faces a far higher risk of dying before the age of five. The economist Branko Milanovic has estimated that the country you live in explains more than half of the variation in income across the world's population. He calls the advantage of being born in a rich country a **citizenship premium**.

On Day 82 you met Rawls's argument that natural and social luck should not determine life chances within a society. But what about the biggest lottery of all, the one that assigns you a country? This lesson asks whether justice, in the full demanding sense, applies between nations or only within them, whether states may close their borders, and what we owe to strangers far away.

sections.heading: Cosmopolitans and Statists
sections.body:
The word **cosmopolitan** comes from the Greek *kosmopolitēs*, 'citizen of the cosmos'. According to Diogenes Laertius, when Diogenes the Cynic (Day 23) was asked where he came from, he replied that he was a citizen of the world. The Stoics (Days 25–26) developed the idea: every human being belongs to a universal community of reason. The Stoic Hierocles pictured each person at the centre of concentric circles (self, family, fellow citizens, humanity) and urged us to draw the outer circles inward.

In modern political philosophy, **moral cosmopolitanism** is the view that every human being has equal moral standing, and that this standing does not depend on nationality. Almost everyone accepts a weak version: it is wrong to torture foreigners. The live debate is over **cosmopolitanism about justice**: do the demanding principles of *distributive* justice, which govern how wealth and opportunity are shared, apply to the whole world?

On the other side are **statists** (sometimes called relationalists). They hold that distributive justice arises only among people who share a certain relationship, typically membership of one state. We owe foreigners humanitarian help and respect for human rights, but not equality.

The clearest statist argument comes from Thomas Nagel in *The Problem of Global Justice* (2005). Nagel argues that the demand for equality arises because a state *coerces* its citizens in their name: you are both subject to its laws and, as a citizen, one of its co-authors. That special relationship requires justifying inequalities to each member. Since there is no world state, there is no comparable relationship globally, and so no global requirement of equality.

Rawls himself, in *The Law of Peoples* (1999), refused to extend his difference principle worldwide. He held that well-ordered peoples have a **duty of assistance** to help 'burdened societies' build decent institutions, but not a duty to equalise wealth once that is achieved. Many of his students thought he had betrayed his own logic.

sections.heading: Pogge: Poverty as Harm
sections.body:
The German-born philosopher **Thomas Pogge**, a student of Rawls, took the debate in a new direction in *World Poverty and Human Rights* (2002).

Most discussions of global poverty frame it as a question of **positive duties**, duties to help, like Peter Singer's drowning child (Day 83). Such duties are contested: how much must I sacrifice for strangers? Pogge's strategy was to argue from a premise even libertarians accept: the **negative duty** not to harm others, and not to impose unjust institutions on them.

His claim is that the global institutional order, the rules about trade, sovereignty, borrowing, intellectual property and resource sales, is shaped by wealthy states and foreseeably produces avoidable severe poverty. By upholding this order, citizens of rich countries are not just failing to help; they are participating in harm.

Two examples make this concrete.

- The **international resource privilege**. Under current international practice, whoever controls a country by force is recognised as entitled to sell its natural resources. Suppose a general seizes power in a coup. He can sell the nation's oil, and foreign buyers acquire legally valid ownership. This gives him the money to buy weapons and loyalty, and gives every would-be general an incentive to try a coup. Pogge links this to the so-called **resource curse**, the observed tendency of some resource-rich poor countries to suffer worse governance.
- The **international borrowing privilege**. A ruler who seizes power can borrow money in the country's name, and later democratic governments are expected to repay. This saddles populations with debts from regimes they never chose.

Pogge also points to rich countries' agricultural subsidies and trade barriers, which make it harder for poor farmers to compete, and to global patent rules that keep medicines expensive.

Critics, such as Mathias Risse, argue that Pogge overstates the role of global rules and understates domestic factors like governance and history; they note that hundreds of millions have escaped extreme poverty in recent decades *within* the existing order. Pogge replies that progress could have been far faster, and that the existence of improvement does not show the rules are just.

sections.heading: Borders: The Case for Opening Them
sections.body:
If justice has a global scope, what about the most visible institution of all, the border?

In a 1987 article, *Aliens and Citizens: The Case for Open Borders*, the Canadian-American philosopher **Joseph Carens** argued that citizenship in a wealthy Western democracy is the modern equivalent of **feudal privilege**: an inherited status that greatly enhances one's life chances and is defended by force. Like noble birth, it is morally arbitrary. Carens argued that whichever major theory you begin from, the conclusion is the same.

- **Rawlsian**: behind a global veil of ignorance, not knowing your birthplace, you would insist on freedom of movement as a basic liberty, since it might be your only route out of poverty or persecution.
- **Libertarian**: if a farmer wants to hire a Mexican worker and the worker wants the job, by what right does the state forbid this voluntary contract?
- **Utilitarian**: economists estimate that freer migration would greatly increase world output, since workers moving from low- to high-productivity places become far more productive.

Carens does not say there can never be limits; security and public order may justify some. But he holds that the presumption is for freedom of movement. After all, most liberal democracies already treat freedom of movement *within* their territory as a basic right. Why should the line stop at the border?

The libertarian philosopher Michael Huemer offered a vivid analogy. A man named Marvin is starving and walks toward a marketplace to buy food from willing sellers. You physically block his path, and he starves. You have not merely failed to help; you have actively harmed him. Huemer argues that immigration restrictions on poor people seeking work are like this.

sections.heading: Borders: The Case for the Right to Exclude
sections.body:
Defenders of a state's right to control immigration offer several arguments.

**Self-determination.** Michael Walzer, whom you met in Lesson 2, argued in *Spheres of Justice* that the power to decide membership is at the core of being a political community. Without it there could be no communities of character, historically stable and with a distinctive way of life. He compared states to clubs, though he also said they are more like families, with special obligations to kin abroad and to refugees.

**Freedom of association.** Christopher Heath Wellman (2008) argued that just as an individual has the right to choose whom to marry or associate with, a legitimate state has a right to choose its members. You may not force your way into a private club or a marriage. Critics reply that refusing a marriage proposal does not keep anyone in poverty, whereas closing a border may.

**National culture and solidarity.** **David Miller**, in *On Nationality* (1995) and *Strangers in Our Midst* (2016), argues that nations are real ethical communities whose members share a public culture and owe each other special obligations. Welfare states depend on trust and solidarity among citizens. Rapid large-scale immigration, he argues, can strain this, so democracies may legitimately set limits, while respecting a strong duty to admit refugees and to treat migrants fairly once admitted.

**Effects on the poor at home.** Some argue that immigration may depress wages for the lowest-paid native workers. The economic evidence here is contested; many studies find small effects either way.

Notice the shape of the debate. Almost no one defends *closed* borders, and almost no one defends total abolition of borders tomorrow. The serious disagreement concerns the presumption: must states justify every exclusion to those excluded (Carens), or may they decide membership as an exercise of democratic self-determination, within humanitarian limits (Miller, Walzer)?

sections.heading: Patriotism, Cosmopolitanism and Nussbaum
sections.body:
Is it wrong to care more about your compatriots? In a 1994 essay, *Patriotism and Cosmopolitanism*, the American philosopher **Martha Nussbaum** argued that education should aim at world citizenship, drawing on the Stoics. National boundaries, she wrote, are morally arbitrary, and pride in one's nation can become a dangerous substitute for concern for human beings as such.

Critics responded that people need particular attachments to live meaningful lives, and that abstract love of humanity motivates few. Most contemporary cosmopolitans accept a compromise: **moderate cosmopolitanism** allows special concern for compatriots, family and friends, as long as everyone's basic human rights and needs are met. Partiality is permitted, but only within a framework that is fair to all. Nussbaum herself later wrote more sympathetically about a purified, inclusive patriotism.

Nussbaum's most influential contribution to global justice, though, is the **capabilities approach**, developed with the Indian economist **Amartya Sen** (Nobel Prize in Economics, 1998). Sen asked what we should measure when we compare how well off people are. Income? It tells you little about whether a disabled person can get around, or whether a woman is allowed to work. Happiness? People adapt to deprivation and may report contentment with very little, what Sen called **adaptive preferences**.

Instead, Sen proposed measuring **capabilities**: people's real freedoms to achieve **functionings**, the beings and doings they have reason to value: being nourished, being literate, taking part in community life. A fasting monk and a starving famine victim have the same functioning (not eating) but very different capabilities: the monk could eat and chooses not to.

Nussbaum went further than Sen and proposed a list of ten **central human capabilities** that every government should guarantee to a threshold level: life; bodily health; bodily integrity; senses, imagination and thought; emotions; practical reason; affiliation; relationship with other species; play; and control over one's political and material environment. Critics ask who has the authority to write such a list, and whether it imposes Western values. Nussbaum answers that her list is deliberately general, open to revision, and justified through cross-cultural dialogue, especially with women's movements in India where she did fieldwork.

sections.heading: From Theory to Institutions
sections.body:
Where does all this lead in practice? Several ideas have moved from seminar rooms into policy.

The capabilities approach directly inspired the United Nations **Human Development Index**, launched in 1990 by the Pakistani economist Mahbub ul Haq with Sen's involvement. It ranks countries not only by income but by life expectancy and education, and has changed how development success is judged.

Pogge has proposed concrete reforms: a **Global Resources Dividend**, a small levy on the extraction of natural resources to fund poverty eradication; and a **Health Impact Fund**, which would reward pharmaceutical companies according to the health impact of their drugs rather than patent monopolies, so that they would have an incentive to develop and cheaply supply medicines for poor countries' diseases.

Anti-corruption and transparency campaigns, such as the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (launched in 2003), which pushes companies and governments to publish payments for oil, gas and minerals, are partly attempts to blunt the resource privilege Pogge identified.

Meanwhile, the **effective altruism** movement, inspired by Singer, has directed large sums to cost-effective global health charities, taking the positive-duty route.

The philosophical disagreements remain. Statists like Nagel worry that cosmopolitan principles without a world government are a demand without an addressee. Cosmopolitans reply that global institutions already exist (trade rules, financial institutions, intellectual property regimes) and already coerce; the question is only whether they are just. Either way, the lesson of this debate is that whether you call global poverty a misfortune or an injustice depends on how you think about institutions, and that answer shapes what you think you owe.

modernConnection.title: Vaccine Nationalism: A Real-World Test of Global Justice
modernConnection.body:
The COVID-19 pandemic forced the abstract debate into the open. When vaccines arrived in late 2020, wealthy countries pre-purchased very large quantities, in some cases far more doses than their populations needed. A global sharing mechanism, **COVAX**, was set up to supply poorer countries, but it struggled for supplies in 2021 while rich nations were vaccinating younger, low-risk groups. Throughout much of 2021, vaccination rates in low-income countries lagged far behind those in high-income countries. In January 2021 the World Health Organization's director-general warned that the world was on the brink of a catastrophic moral failure.

Each theory in this lesson gives a distinct verdict. A **statist** might say a government has a special duty to protect its own citizens first, so pre-purchasing was permissible, though humanitarian duties required sharing surpluses. A **cosmopolitan** might say that vaccinating a healthy 25-year-old in London before an 80-year-old health worker in Lagos wrongly treats nationality as a moral trump card. **Pogge** would focus on institutions: patent rules and export practices that left manufacturing concentrated in a few countries, and the debate over waiving vaccine patents at the World Trade Organization. The **capabilities approach** would ask which allocation best protected everyone's threshold capability for life and bodily health.

There were also self-interested reasons for sharing: the virus does not respect borders, and new variants can arise wherever transmission continues. But notice that self-interest and justice can come apart. Even if sharing had not benefited rich countries at all, cosmopolitans would argue it was owed.

The same structure reappears with climate change, where those least responsible for emissions often face the gravest harms. Global justice is no longer a thought experiment.

vocabulary.definition: The view that every human being has equal moral standing regardless of nationality; in its strong form, that principles of justice apply globally.
vocabulary.example: A cosmopolitan argues that a child's life in Malawi matters exactly as much as a child's life in Manchester.

vocabulary.definition: The view that demanding principles of distributive justice apply only among people who share a state or similar coercive institution.
vocabulary.example: Nagel's statism holds that we owe foreigners humanitarian aid but not economic equality.

vocabulary.definition: Rawls's duty of well-ordered peoples to help burdened societies establish decent institutions.
vocabulary.example: Under the duty of assistance, aid aims to build institutions, not to equalise wealth permanently.

vocabulary.definition: Pogge's term for the international practice of treating whoever controls a country as entitled to sell its natural resources.
vocabulary.example: Because of the international resource privilege, a dictator can legally sell his nation's diamonds.

vocabulary.definition: The large income and life-chance advantage that comes from being born in, or a citizen of, a wealthy country.
vocabulary.example: Carens compares the citizenship premium to inherited feudal privilege.

vocabulary.definition: An approach to justice and development that measures people's real freedoms to do and be what they have reason to value.
vocabulary.example: The capabilities approach asks not how much money a woman has but whether she can actually travel, work and vote.

vocabulary.definition: The actual beings and doings that make up a life, such as being nourished, reading or taking part in community life.
vocabulary.example: Being healthy is a functioning; having access to healthcare and the freedom to use it is a capability.

vocabulary.definition: Desires that have adjusted to unjust or deprived circumstances, so that people come to want little because they expect little.
vocabulary.example: Sen pointed out that adaptive preferences can make deprived people report satisfaction with very poor conditions.

thinkingExercise.title: The Border Hearing
thinkingExercise.prompt: Imagine you sit on a panel deciding a national immigration policy. Before you are three applicants: a refugee fleeing persecution, a skilled engineer seeking higher pay, and an unskilled worker escaping poverty. Work out how each theory would treat them.
steps: Write one sentence on how Carens's open-borders view would treat each applicant.
Now apply Miller's view: what would he say about each, and what limits would he accept?
Apply Pogge: is there any sense in which your country is responsible for the conditions the poor worker is fleeing?
State your own policy for the three applicants and identify the strongest objection to it from the view you rejected. How would you answer that objection?

summary: Cosmopolitans hold that justice reaches across borders; statists like Nagel and Rawls (in The Law of Peoples) limit equality to members of a state, with humanitarian and assistance duties beyond.
Pogge reframes global poverty as harm caused through an unjust global order, citing the resource and borrowing privileges.
Carens argues citizenship in rich states resembles feudal privilege and that freedom of movement should be the presumption.
Walzer, Wellman and Miller defend a qualified right to exclude based on self-determination, association and national solidarity.
Sen and Nussbaum's capabilities approach measures real freedoms to do and be, inspiring the Human Development Index.

quiz.question: Nagel's statist view grounds the demand for equality in which feature of states?
options: Coercive laws imposed in the name of citizens who are also their co-authors
quiz.explanation: For Nagel, the special justificatory burden arises from the state's coercion of its own members in their name.

quiz.question: Pogge argues that affluent citizens' duties toward the global poor are primarily:
options: Negative duties not to uphold institutions that harm them
Duties to their own nation only
quiz.explanation: Pogge's strategy rests on the widely accepted negative duty not to harm, applied to global institutions.

quiz.question: Which situation best illustrates the 'international borrowing privilege'?
options: A democratic government issues bonds for schools
A junta borrows heavily abroad, and a later elected government is expected to repay
A student takes out a loan
A company borrows to build a factory
quiz.explanation: The borrowing privilege lets illegitimate rulers saddle future populations with debts.

quiz.question: Rawls's The Law of Peoples extends the difference principle to the whole world.
quiz.explanation: Rawls rejected a global difference principle, proposing only a duty of assistance to burdened societies.

quiz.question: Carens compares citizenship in rich Western democracies to:
quiz.explanation: Like noble birth, it is an inherited, morally arbitrary status that greatly improves life chances.

quiz.question: Wellman's argument for a state's right to exclude is based mainly on:
quiz.explanation: Wellman argues that legitimate states, like individuals, have a right to choose with whom they associate.

quiz.question: David Miller holds that states may limit immigration but still have strong duties toward refugees.
quiz.explanation: Miller defends national self-determination while affirming duties to refugees and fair treatment of admitted migrants.

quiz.question: A fasting monk and a famine victim both eat nothing. In Sen's terms, they share the same:
quiz.explanation: Their functioning (not eating) is the same, but their capabilities differ: the monk could choose to eat.

quiz.question: The Human Development Index was inspired chiefly by:
quiz.explanation: Mahbub ul Haq developed the HDI drawing on Sen's capabilities approach, measuring health and education alongside income.

quiz.question: Moderate cosmopolitanism forbids any special concern for one's own compatriots.
quiz.explanation: Moderate cosmopolitans allow partiality as long as everyone's basic rights and needs are secured.

goDeeper.body:
A powerful middle path in this debate is the **relational** view of Joshua Cohen and Charles Sabel, and the 'practice-dependent' approach of Aaron James and Andrea Sangiovanni. They agree with statists that justice depends on relationships, but deny that only the state counts. Global trade, for example, is a cooperative practice with its own rules, gains and losses. If so, principles of fairness apply to it, even without a world government: for instance, rich countries may not structure trade rules so that the gains flow overwhelmingly to themselves. On this view, global justice is neither nothing (as strict statists suggest) nor a full global difference principle (as some cosmopolitans claim), but a patchwork of standards tied to particular institutions: the World Trade Organization, the global financial system, climate agreements.

Another frontier concerns **climate refugees**. International refugee law, based on the 1951 Refugee Convention, protects those fleeing persecution, not environmental disaster. Some philosophers argue that if wealthy countries' emissions have helped make a homeland uninhabitable, the case for admission becomes one of compensation, not charity. This links Pogge's harm-based reasoning to Carens's freedom of movement. Small island states facing sea-level rise make the question concrete.

Finally, Kwame Anthony Appiah's *Cosmopolitanism: Ethics in a World of Strangers* (2006) offers a gentler cosmopolitanism grounded in conversation across difference rather than a single universal theory, a bridge to the next track's world philosophies.

readings.title: World Poverty and Human Rights
readings.author: Thomas Pogge
readings.note: Chapters 1 and 4 present the harm argument and the resource and borrowing privileges.

readings.title: The Ethics of Immigration
readings.author: Joseph Carens
readings.note: A mature book-length version of his case for open borders, with careful discussion of real policy.

readings.title: Creating Capabilities
readings.author: Martha Nussbaum
readings.note: A short, accessible introduction to the capabilities approach and the list of central capabilities.

readings.title: Strangers in Our Midst
readings.author: David Miller
readings.note: The most careful defence of a democratic right to control immigration.

questions: If your country's wealth partly depends on rules that harm the poor abroad, what follows for you as an individual citizen?
Is a state's right to control its borders more like a person's right to choose a spouse, or like a landowner's right to block a starving man?
Could a single list of central capabilities be fair to every culture?
